newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: INTERVIEW - Funding key to Sierra Rutile reopening.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Funding key to Sierra Rutile reopening.

text.p: Sierra Leone's rutile mine, one of the mainstays of the economy until rebels halted operations in 1995, should reopen in 1997 but much will depened on funding, the chief executive of the company that owns it says.

"We still hope to reopen next year, although we cannot be specific about the date. The issue now, more than anything else, is a financial one," Sierra Rutile chief executive Brian Calver told Reuters by telephone from Britain.
"A lot of our lenders' concerns are commercial ones, as well as the political and security situation in the country," he added in the interview on Monday.
The civilian government which took over in March is keen to revive the shattered economy.

"The contribution of rutile to our economy was absolutely vital and I believe it will once again be of key importance in the short term," Sierra Leone Central Bank governor Steve Swaray told Reuters. "I say short term because of the problem of land degradation," he added.
Rutile or titanium dioxide is of strategic importance in the aerospace industry and is also used in paint pigment.

Sierra Rutile, the world's second largest producer of the commodity when the rebels attacked, is owned by U.S. firm Nord Resources Corp and Australian-based Consolidated Rutile Ltd. At one stage it had hoped to reopen the mine, 120 km southeast of the capital Freetown, by October.

Calver, who estimated the cost of putting the mine back into working order at $80 million, said shareholders had just held a board meeting in Singapore. "There will have to be compromise between the banks and the shareholders, but I am optimistic that the situation will be resolved quickly," he said.
The International Monetary Fund and World Bank have been calling for foreign investment in the rutile sector as part of the country's structural adjustment programme.
Calver said in May the World Bank and the IMF had agreed an $18 million loan for rehabilitation. Their International Finance Corporation is one source of funding.
Minerals provide most of the country's export earnings.
Sierra Rutile provided 57 percent of Sierra Leone's mineral export earnings, which totalled $108 million in 1993.
Consolidated Rutile bought a 50 percent stake in Sierra Rutile in 1994, with the aim of expanding operations.
In 1994, Sierra Rutile's investment in Sierra Leone totalled about $100 million and it employed 1,800. In the year to June 1994 it produced 144,000 tonnes, a quarter of the world total.
Rebels overran the mine in January 1995 along with the Sierra Leone Ore and Metal Co (SIEROMCO) southern bauxite mine. They held 17 foreign nationals for over three months.

SIEROMCO's Managing Director James Westwood said last week the company would be pulling out of the country as reopening its Mokanji mine was not viable. But he said the sale of the mine to other investors had not been ruled out.
Sierra Rutile has told the government it wants to make independent security arrangements in the short term.

Private South African security company Executive Outcomes, which previously trained the Sierra Leone army to fight the rebels and whose staff are denounced by critics as mercenaries, guards its mine through a subsidiary called Lifeguard.

President Ahmad Tejan Kabbah and rebel leader Foday Sankoh have agreed a truce but differences over a role for the rebels and their demands for all foreign troops to leave have blocked a permanent deal.
The rebels count Executive Outcomes as foreign troops.

"As long as the president is comfortable with us using Lifeguard in the short-term, I think it is sensible as they are more than able for the job, but it is unlikely in the long term and we wouldn't do anything against Kabbah's wishes," Calver said.
